text:
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Linux CLI Execution and Stream Redirection",
    "scope": "Introduces foundational command-line execution concepts in Unix-like operating systems. Covers directory creation, running commands as background processes, and manipulating standard output streams. Establishes the command-line interface for invoking the GNU Compiler Collection.",
    "key_points": [
      "Directory creation using `mkdir <folder_name>`",
      "Asynchronous background execution using the trailing ampersand `&`",
      "Standard output redirection: file overwrite `>` versus append `>>`",
      "Basic C compilation and binary naming syntax: `gcc ex.c -o ex`"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "Structural Architecture of a C Source Program",
    "scope": "Deconstructs the formal anatomy and layout of standard C source files. Differentiates between required and optional program sections according to language standards. Explains the execution entry point and division of responsibility within the primary runtime function.",
    "key_points": [
      "Six structural sections: Documentation, Link (`#include`), Definition (`#define`), Global declaration, `main()` function, and Subprograms",
      "Every valid C program strictly requires exactly one `main()` function section; all other sections are optional",
      "Internal structure of `main()`: declaration part followed by executable part",
      "User-defined function definitions housed within the subprogram section"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "Variable Model, Identifiers, and Scope Classifications",
    "scope": "Defines a program variable as an abstraction over hardware memory cells and details its six governing attributes. Specifies strict identifier naming syntax and invalid token rules. Classifies variable accessibility into three distinct architectural scopes.",
    "key_points": [
      "Six variable characteristics: name (identifier), type (value domain), address (memory location), value (current state), lifetime (temporal existence), and scope (spatial visibility)",
      "Identifier lexical grammar: must begin with an alphabetic letter or underscore `_`; digits and typographical symbols (`#`, `*`, etc.) are invalid starting characters; language keywords cannot serve as identifiers",
      "Three variable scope tiers: global variables (declared outside all functions), local variables (declared within a function block), and formal parameters (declared in function signatures)",
      "Stack lifetime and function accessibility constraints governing local variables versus globals"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "C Type System, Memory Footprints, and Numeral Bases",
    "scope": "Classifies primitive and derived data types in C and details their physical memory allocations. Covers the `sizeof` operator, type conversion rules, and truncation pitfalls during type casting. Explains numeric representations across decimal, binary, octal, and hexadecimal bases.",
    "key_points": [
      "Primitive types: signed/unsigned `char`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `long long`, `float`, `double`, `long double`, and `void`",
      "Derived types: single- and multi-dimensional arrays, strings (null-terminated character sequences), structures, unions, and pointers",
      "Compile-time memory sizing via `sizeof(type)` or `sizeof(variable)` yielding size in bytes (e.g., typical 32/64-bit systems: `int` = 4 bytes, `float` = 4 bytes, `double` = 8 bytes)",
      "Floating-point representation (significand and exponent) versus fixed-width integer capacity; truncation and overflow during narrowing casts",
      "Positional numeral systems: base-2 (binary), base-8 (octal), base-10 (decimal), and base-16 (hexadecimal)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "Standard Streams, I/O Mechanics, and Buffer Safety",
    "scope": "Details stream-based input and output facilities provided by standard C libraries. Analyzes memory corruption vulnerabilities inherent to unconstrained input routines and presents secure, bounded alternatives. Examines command-line argument passing semantics via the main function signature.",
    "key_points": [
      "Character stream I/O functions (`getchar`, `putchar`, `fgetc`, `fputc`, `puts`, `fputs`) versus formatted I/O (`printf`, `fprintf`, `scanf`, `fscanf`)",
      "Buffer overflow vulnerability in unbounded reading functions: `gets()` and unqualified `%s` in `scanf()`",
      "Safe input ingestion with bounded stream reads: `fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), stdin)`",
      "Portability constraints of POSIX-specific `getline()` across operating systems",
      "Formatted in-memory conversions: string-to-numeric using `sscanf()` and numeric-to-string using `sprintf()`",
      "Command-line arguments: `int argc` (argument count) and `char *argv[]` (array of argument string pointers, with `argv[0]` storing program name)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Pointers, Memory Addressing, and Low-Level System Control",
    "scope": "Introduces the pointer data type as a direct representation of physical or virtual memory addresses. Explains address-of and dereferencing operators alongside memory stack progression diagrams. Highlights why explicit memory access makes C optimal for operating systems while contrasting its lack of high-level runtime features.",
    "key_points": [
      "Pointer definition: a typed variable holding the memory address of a variable or data structure",
      "Address-of operator `&` (obtaining memory location) and dereference operator `*` (accessing value at memory location)",
      "Stack state transitions across pointer declaration, address assignment (`p = &c1`), and indirect modification (`c2 = *p`)",
      "Features deliberately omitted from C: classes, objects, packages, threads, strict type safety, and automatic garbage collection",
      "Manual dynamic memory lifecycle: explicit heap allocation with `malloc()` and release with `free()`; avoidance of non-deterministic garbage collection pauses in kernel code"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "Parameter Passing Semantics: By-Value versus By-Reference",
    "scope": "Contrasts the functional and architectural mechanics of passing data across function call frames. Examines how value copying protects local state and how pointer passing enables mutable caller state. Illustrates stack frame interactions for both evaluation models.",
    "key_points": [
      "Pass-by-value semantics: formal parameter receives an isolated copy of the argument value; mutations inside the callee leave caller variables unmodified",
      "Pass-by-reference semantics (implemented via pointers): formal parameter receives the memory address of the argument",
      "Calley dereferencing (`*param = *param + 1`) to mutate original caller memory directly across stack frames",
      "Memory efficiency and side-effect control when designing function interfaces"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "The C Preprocessor and Modular Header Design",
    "scope": "Covers the syntax and operational role of the C preprocessor before code enters the compilation phase. Teaches header file inclusion mechanics, directory search path rules, and modular software decomposition. Explains how symbolic constants replace raw literals for safety and performance.",
    "key_points": [
      "Preprocessor directive rules: lines beginning with `#`, lack of terminating semicolons, and line continuation using trailing backslash `\\`",
      "Header inclusion formats: `#include <file.h>` (system include path) versus `#include \"file.h\"` (current working directory / user-defined search paths)",
      "Modularization benefits of `.h` header files: clear component interfaces, separate module testing/verification, and compiler mock contracts",
      "Symbolic constant definition `#define IDENTIFIER TOKEN`: literal token replacement, avoiding hardcoded magic numbers, and compiler optimization advantages over public mutable variables"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 9,
    "title": "Macro Substitution Mechanics and Operator Precedence Hazards",
    "scope": "Explores parameterized function-like macros and their execution via direct textual substitution without type inspection. Identifies arithmetic precedence bugs and unintended syntax alterations caused by unparenthesized macro arguments. Details the critical flaw of side-effect duplication.",
    "key_points": [
      "Function-like macro definition: `#define macro_name(params) token_string` eliminating function call runtime overhead",
      "Mechanism of pure textual substitution without semantic evaluation or syntax tree validation",
      "Precedence bugs in composite expressions: e.g., `#define plus(x,y) x+y` yielding `plus(a,b)*2 -> a + b * 2` instead of `(a + b) * 2`",
      "Parenthesization rules: wrapping both the entire macro body and individual parameter occurrences, e.g., `#define times(x, y) ((x)*(y))`",
      "Side-effect hazard: argument re-evaluation in multi-occurrence macros (e.g., `#define double(x) ((x)+(x))` expanding `double(b++)` to `((b++)+(b++))` causing unintended double increments)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 10,
    "title": "Conditional Compilation and Architectural Portability",
    "scope": "Focuses on preprocessor directives that conditionally include or exclude blocks of source code based on build flags. Explains how conditional compilation isolates architecture-specific hardware routines. Establishes the mechanism of cross-compilation across heterogeneous CPU architectures.",
    "key_points": [
      "Conditional directives: `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#if`, `#else`, and `#endif`",
      "Code gating: preprocessor eliminates inactive branches prior to compiler pass, reducing executable size and preventing unsupported instruction compilation",
      "Isolating architecture-dependent hardware interactions (e.g., x86 interrupt acknowledgments `intel_int_ack()` vs. SPARC operations)",
      "Cross-architectural compilation management using preprocessor flags"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 11,
    "title": "The Multi-Stage C Compilation Pipeline",
    "scope": "Follows the transformation of C source text into executable machine code through four sequential system toolchain stages. Details file extensions, artifact formats, and the responsibilities of the preprocessor, compiler, assembler, and linker. Introduces modern compiler frameworks and intermediate representations.",
    "key_points": [
      "Preprocessing stage: takes `.c` and `.h` files, expands macros and includes, outputs extended source `.i`",
      "Compilation stage: translates preprocessed `.i` code into target-specific assembly code `.s` or `.asm`",
      "Assembly stage: translates assembly instructions into relocatable binary machine instructions, outputting object files (`.o` or `.obj`)",
      "Linking stage: combines multiple object files with static/shared libraries (e.g., `libc.a`), resolves external and inter-function references, relocates machine addresses, and produces final executable (`a.out` or binary)",
      "OS Loader: transfers executable from persistent disk storage into main memory as an active process",
      "LLVM infrastructure: multi-target compilation via low-level intermediate representation (IR)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 12,
    "title": "Build Automation, Dependency Tracking, and Makefiles",
    "scope": "Teaches the theory and implementation of incremental compilation in large-scale system software projects. Explains dependency tracking using file modification timestamps to minimize recompilation overhead. Contrasts manual Makefiles with automated meta-build generation tools.",
    "key_points": [
      "Cost of full rebuilds in large codebases when modifying shared header files included across multiple compilation units",
      "Dependency graph modeling in `Makefile`: mapping targets, prerequisites, and build rules",
      "Timestamp-based change detection: `make` compares the last modified timestamps of target object files against their dependent source/header files",
      "Targeted re-compilation: only rebuilding modified `.c` files and relinking dependencies",
      "Automated build system generators: `cmake` as an abstraction layer to generate native Makefiles without manual syntax errors"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 13,
    "title": "Process Runtime Memory Layout and OS Execution Models",
    "scope": "Models the virtual address space organization of an operating system or program process at runtime. Explains the structural roles, mutability, and growth vectors of memory segments. Highlights direct CPU execution of operating systems in contrast to interpreted or JIT-compiled runtimes.",
    "key_points": [
      "Text (code) segment: read-only, immutable region positioned near lower virtual memory containing raw CPU instructions",
      "Data segment: positioned above the text segment, holding initialized and uninitialized global/static variables with upward growth capability",
      "Stack segment: allocated at high virtual memory addresses, growing downward as function activation frames are pushed and shrinking upon returns",
      "Dynamic kernel loading: loading modular device drivers and file system modules post-boot into running memory",
      "Direct hardware execution: operating system binaries execute natively on bare CPU hardware without interpreter layers or JIT compilation engines"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 14,
    "title": "System Metric Scaling and Prefix Standards",
    "scope": "Catalogs the international standard decimal metric units utilized for hardware timing, memory capacities, bus speeds, and resource measurements in computer operating systems. Defines the full hierarchy of negative and positive powers of ten prefixes from yocto through yotta.",
    "key_points": [
      "Sub-unit system time/latency prefixes: milli ($10^{-3}$), micro ($10^{-6}$), nano ($10^{-9}$), pico ($10^{-12}$), femto ($10^{-15}$), atto ($10^{-18}$), zepto ($10^{-21}$), and yocto ($10^{-24}$)",
      "Super-unit scale/throughput prefixes: kilo ($10^{3}$), mega ($10^{6}$), giga ($10^{9}$), tera ($10^{12}$), peta ($10^{15}$), exa ($10^{18}$), zetta ($10^{21}$), and yotta ($10^{24}$)",
      "Relevance to hardware characterization: CPU clock periods in nanoseconds/picoseconds, system bus frequencies in megahertz/gigahertz, storage in gigabytes/terabytes"
    ]
  }
]
